query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor microalloying addition of less than 3 atomic percent of copper (Cu) into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy will induce the in-situ formation of ductile, nano-scale precipitates at the grain boundaries. This modification is expected to impede crack initiation and propagation, thereby enhancing mechanical integrity while largely preserving the caloric response driven by the martensitic/magneto-structural transformation.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy in its as-synthesized bulk state showing a large caloric effect but suffering from poor mechanical integrity and cracking.
generation.intervention: Add a minor microalloying element (e.g., <3 at% Cu) during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: The material will be subjected to applied magnetic and pressure fields along with thermal cycling through the phase transition and cyclic mechanical loading. Testing conditions should mirror those used in caloric performance assessments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of finely dispersed, ductile nanoprecipitates at the grain boundaries resulting from Cu segregation.
generation.mechanism: The Cu addition is proposed to segregate to the grain boundaries and initiate the formation of nano-precipitates. These precipitates refine the grain boundary structure and increase resistance to crack initiation and propagation while the matrix retains its crystallographic features essential for the caloric effect, thus maintaining overall caloric performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement in compressive strength by an estimated 20–50% and reduced cracking incidents, while the caloric response is altered by less than 5% compared to the untouched alloy.
generation.baseline: The original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits a large caloric effect but has low mechanical integrity and is prone to cracking.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under similar field conditions (magnetic and pressure), temperature ranges across the caloric phase transition, and cyclic loading regimes used in standard caloric tests. It must also remain applicable without introducing rare-earth elements.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative changes in mechanical properties and any minor effects on the caloric response require experimental verification, and the precise dispersion and stability of the Cu-induced nano-precipitates under operational conditions remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples under identical processing conditions: one set with a <3 at% Cu addition and one without (control). Subject both sample sets to identical magnetic and pressure field applications, thermal cycling across their phase transitions, and cyclic mechanical loading. Characterize both sets for compressive strength, crack propagation behavior, and caloric performance using standardized mechanical tests and caloric effect measurements.
measurements: Crack initiation and propagation metrics (e.g., number and size of cracks)
Caloric response magnitude (e.g., temperature change under field cycling)
Hysteresis and reversibility of the caloric effect
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-microalloyed samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than 20% increase in compressive strength or no reduction in cracking) while maintaining the caloric response within ±5% of the control alloy, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. As a result, precipitation strengthening should be considered in developing HEAs for high temperature applications. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. However, most of these RHEAs are generally characterized with high density and poor high temperature oxidation

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

frame.system: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy in its as-synthesized bulk state, exhibiting a martensitic or magneto-structural transition responsible for its caloric effect
frame.goal: Achieve robust mechanical integrity (i.e. enhanced resistance to cracking and higher compressive strength) without reducing its large caloric response under applied fields and pressures
frame.limitation: The alloy, while showing a strong caloric effect, tends to crack and exhibits poor integrity; previous composite approaches have only partially improved strength or thermal transport, but not both simultaneously
root_cause_cues: desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved
constraints: The intervention must be a single, non-composite modification
It must preserve the high caloric effect (magneto-structural response)
The alloy should remain rare-earth free
Operability under applied-field and pressure-field conditions must be maintained
frame.regime: Operates under conditions of applied magnetic and/or pressure fields, with temperature and loading regimes typical of caloric effect testing (i.e., cyclical mechanical loading and thermal cycling across the phase transition)
prior_attempts: Epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe composites yielding compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at different epoxy loadings
Low-melting indium composites achieving only 48 MPa compressive strength while enhancing thermal conductivity
frame.hypothesis: Introduce a minor microalloying addition that promotes in-situ nanostructured precipitation to toughen the material. For example, adding a small (<3 at%) quantity of a ductile, first-row transition metal (such as Cu or possibly a controlled amount of Ti known to refine grain boundaries) could lead to finely dispersed, ductile precipitates at grain boundaries, which hinder crack initiation and propagation without disrupting the crystallographic features responsible for the large caloric response. The mechanism would involve grain-boundary segregation and nanoprecipitate formation that refines the microstructure and enhances ductility, leading to an expected improvement in compressive strength by 20–50% while altering the caloric performance by less than 5%. Boundary conditions for testing would include the same applied magnetic/pressure fields, temperatures spanning the phase transition, and mechanical load cycling. Prior evidence from high-entropy alloy literature supports that microalloying to refine microstructure and promote ductile phase dispersion can enhance toughness without significantly affecting multifunctional properties. A decisive controlled experiment would entail preparing otherwise identical batches of the alloy with and without the microalloying addition, then performing a series of mechanical (compressive strength, crack propagation) and caloric performance tests. If the microalloyed sample does not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity while maintaining the caloric response (or if the caloric response diminishes notably), the hypothesis would be falsified.

decision.trend: Early studies on high-entropy and multifunctional materials first addressed mechanical limitations by incorporating secondary phases using ex situ composite routes. For instance, epoxy and low-melting indium composites were applied to similar MM′X materials to independently boost either compressive strength or heat transport. Parallel work on refractory HEAs (PMC7513042) and precipitation‐strengthened alloys (PMC10213035) later demonstrated that tailoring the in‐situ microstructure—via controlled precipitation and phase architecture—can dramatically enhance mechanical properties. However, these improvements were not simultaneously achieved with retention of the desired functional (caloric) response, leaving a gap when both robust integrity and magneto-structural performance are required.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved challenge is to simultaneously increase the bulk mechanical integrity (crack resistance and compressive strength) and maintain the large caloric response intrinsic to the martensitic/magneto-structural transformation, all while avoiding rare-earth additions. Previous composite strategies improved individual metrics but compromised either the interface quality or functional performance.
decision.why: Introducing a minor (<3 at%) addition of a ductile, first‐row transition metal (e.g., Cu) is predicted to promote in-situ nanostructured precipitation that refines the grain boundaries and impedes crack propagation. This mechanism, supported by trends in HEA literature where controlled nanoprecipitation enhances toughness without materially altering the crystallography that drives the caloric effect, would likely boost compressive strength by 20–50% while altering the caloric performance by less than 5%. The intervention is designed to operate under the same applied magnetic/pressure fields, temperature cycling, and mechanical loading conditions used in caloric testing. A decisive controlled experiment would compare the original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with a microalloyed variant under identical conditions; a failure to observe a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity or a notable degradation in caloric effect would falsify the hypothesis.
